screens.title: Project 3: Memory and the Program Counter
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will complete the Hack computer's memory subsystem and build the components that let a C P U remember values and step through instructions. We will move from a single Bit and a 16-bit Register to a family of R A M chips built recursively, culminating in RAM16K as the Hack data memory. You will also assemble the Program Counter, which chooses between holding its value, loading a new address, incrementing, or resetting to zero. These pieces are essential because memory and the program counter control program flow and data storage in the von Neumann architecture. For example, when executing a jump instruction the C P U asserts the PC's load input so the next instruction comes from a new address; when starting the system the reset input ensures execution begins at address zero. As you build each R A M level, you'll see the same small building blocks repeated and combined using DMux and Mux chips to route addresses and data. By the end of Project 3 you will have tested read/write isolation, correct uninitialized behavior, and the PC selection priority. Think about why reset must override load and increment — that's the safety that lets a machine recover to a known state.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Project 3 Overview
16:9 HD Classroom

Project 3: Memory & PC

Complete the sequential chips that form data memory and build the Program Counter that advances and controls instruction flow. Learn the recursive RAM structure and the PC's prioritized selection chain.

Lab walkthrough style: steps, checks, and tests
In this lesson
Build Bit→Register→RAM hierarchy; assemble the PC; pass RAM tests ensuring isolation and correct uninitialized reads.
Why it matters
Memory and the program counter are the heart of sequential execution. Without correct memory, programs cannot store variables or jump reliably.
Coming up
Register & Bit
Build 16-bit storage from single-bit registers.
Recursive RAM
Assemble RAM8→RAM64→...→RAM16K with Mux/DMux trees.
Program Counter
Implement inc, load, reset with correct priority.
Visual snapshot
Bit → Register
RAM hierarchy (recursive)
PC with priority chain
Key takeaway
Small, tested sequential chips combine predictably into large memories. The PC enforces safe control flow by prioritizing reset and load over increment.
Starter checklist
  • Implement Bit and Register
  • Assemble RAM8 then build up recursively
  • Build PC and verify priority reset & load

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of Project 3 you will have four verified competencies. First, you will complete the sequential chips that the Hack C P U needs to hold state: implement the Bit primitive and the 16-bit Register and understand how load gates control writing on the clock. Second, you will assemble the R A M family up to RAM16K by composing smaller R A M chips recursively; you will explain how lower and upper address bits are used to select the right subchip. Third, you will design and test the Program Counter with three controls — increment, load, and reset — and understand why the reset > load > inc priority is essential for predictable startup and jumps. Fourth, you will prepare for higher-level architecture work by ensuring your memory components pass tests for uninitialized reads, write isolation, and sequential read/write behavior. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic and a verified competency milestone you can use as a checkpoint in the simulator.

screens.title: Bit and 16-bit Register
screens.narratorSegment: Begin with the Bit primitive: a single flip-flop that stores one binary value across clock cycles. In the Hack design the Bit is built from a D flip-flop with a Mux that selects between the existing value and the input gated by the load signal. That small pattern is the building block for registers. A 16-bit Register is simply sixteen Bit chips wired in parallel, all sharing the same load and clock signals so they write together. Concretely, when load is 1 the Mux forwards the D inputs into the flip-flops on the rising clock edge; when load is 0 each Bit feeds back its current output, so the register holds its previous value. A common misconception is thinking each bit can be written independently inside a register; in this design the entire 16-bit vector updates together under a single load. A practical example: to store the constant address 123 into a register, set the register's input bus to the 16-bit representation of 123 and assert load for one clock tick—after the tick the register holds 123. Key checks while implementing: confirm each Bit holds its state when load is 0, and that toggling load writes all 16 bits in sync. Takeaway: small, verified flip-flops compose predictably into wider registers.

keyIdea.title: Register insight
keyIdea.text: A 16-bit register is 16 synchronized Bit chips; load controls whether the register writes new inputs or holds the current value.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Bit & Register
Definition

Bit primitive and 16-bit Register

A Bit is a D flip-flop with a Mux controlled by load. Sixteen Bits wired in parallel form a 16-bit Register.

Implementation notes
  • Each Bit has inputs: in, load, clock and output: out.
  • Register shares load and clock across 16 Bits to update synchronously.
  • When load is 0, the feedback path holds the previous value.
Visual: parallel bits
Bit chip
DFF + Mux. Inputs: in, load. Output: out.
16-bit Register
16 Bits with shared load/clock. Writes occur simultaneously across bits when load=1.
Example
To store the address 123, place its 16-bit pattern on the input bus and assert load for one clock tick. After the tick the register returns that value on its output until the next write.
Common mistake
Assuming individual bits can be loaded independently; here the whole 16-bit register updates together under one load control.

screens.title: Constructing RAM8 and Address Selection
screens.narratorSegment: RAM8 is the first composite R A M chip: it contains eight 16-bit registers and an address width of three bits. The three-bit address directly selects which of the eight registers drives the output and which register receives a write. This selection is implemented with DMuxes that split the load signal by address and with Muxes that combine each register's output into a single 16-bit bus. The pattern is straightforward: the lower-level registers are identical, and DMux logic ensures only the targeted register sees the load on a write cycle. A concrete example: if address 010 is presented and load is 1 during the clock, the DMux routes the load to register number two; that register latches the input value while the others hold. A common misconception is thinking Muxes copy values in hardware; rather they steer buses so only the selected register's output appears on the shared output bus. In practice, implement RAM8 by instantiating eight Register chips, use a 3-way DMux tree for write selection, and a 3-way Mux tree for read aggregation. Takeaway: RAM8 shows the basic pattern you will replicate recursively to build larger R A M chips.

keyIdea.title: RAM8 pattern
keyIdea.text: Use DMux to route write-enable by address and Mux to select the output; this exact pattern repeats in larger RAM chips.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › RAM8 Construction
Process

Build RAM8

RAM8 uses eight 16-bit registers, 3-bit addressing, DMux for write routing, and Mux for read selection.

Step 1 — Instantiate registers
Create eight 16-bit registers, each with load input driven by a DMux of the RAM load and the 3-bit address.
Step 2 — Route writes with DMux
Use address bits to DMux the single load signal so only the selected register receives load=1.
Step 3 — Aggregate reads with Mux
Combine the eight register outputs with a 8-way Mux controlled by the address to produce the RAM output bus.
Example
Address 010 and load=1: DMux routes load to register 2, that register latches the input value on the clock. All other registers hold their previous values.
Key takeaway
The same DMux/Mux pattern that routes write and read signals at RAM8 will be reused at larger scales.
Misconception
Muxes do not duplicate data; they select which register's output appears on the bus. Only the selected register's data is visible externally.

screens.title: Recursive Construction: RAM64 and Beyond
screens.narratorSegment: The power of recursion becomes clear when you build RAM64 from RAM8 blocks. RAM64 contains eight RAM8 chips and uses a six-bit address. The address is partitioned: the lower three bits select a register within a RAM8 block, and the upper three bits select which of the eight RAM8 chips to enable. On a write, the RAM64 DMux tree uses the upper address bits to route the overall load to exactly one RAM8 chip; that chip's internal DMuxes then route the load to the targeted register inside it. On a read, a two-level Mux tree first selects the output from each RAM8 using the lower bits and then selects among these eight outputs using the upper bits. This approach generalizes: RAM512 uses nine-bit addressing (lower 3 bits intra-chip, upper 6 bits to choose which RAM64 block), and higher levels follow the same split. A concrete example: to write at address 0b001011 you route load to the RAM8 specified by upper bits 001 and inside that RAM8 use lower bits 011 to address the register. A useful mental model is a tree of identical modules: the same small unit repeats at every node. Misunderstanding often comes from confusing which bits are 'upper' vs 'lower'—draw the bit positions to avoid that error. Takeaway: recursion simplifies wiring by reusing tested components and predictable address partitioning.

keyIdea.title: Recursive scaling
keyIdea.text: Large RAM chips are built by composing smaller RAMs; split the address into upper and lower bits to select a subchip and an inner register.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › RAM: Scale by recursion

RAM64 and the recursive pattern

Compose eight RAM8 chips to make RAM64. Split the 6-bit address into upper and lower halves for inter- and intra-chip selection.

Pattern repeats for RAM512, RAM4K, RAM16K
Address split
Lower 3 bits: index inside RAM8. Upper 3 bits: choose which RAM8 block is active in RAM64.
Write flow
Upper bits DMux the write enable to one RAM8; inside that block lower bits select the register to write.
Read flow
Lower bits select outputs from each RAM8; upper bits select which of those outputs becomes the RAM64 output.
Concrete example
Address 0b001011: upper 001 selects the second RAM8; lower 011 selects the fourth register inside that RAM8. Only that register receives the write enable and later drives the output when read.
Tip
When wiring, label address bits clearly and draw upper vs lower partitions to avoid misrouting signals between levels.

screens.title: RAM512 → RAM4K → RAM16K: Scaling the hierarchy
screens.narratorSegment: Scaling beyond RAM64 follows the same architectural pattern: add more address bits and compose larger blocks from smaller ones. RAM512 uses nine address bits and is built from eight RAM64 modules; the lower three bits still select a register within a RAM8, the next three pick the RAM8 inside a RAM64, and the upper three choose which RAM64 block to enable. Continuing this pattern, RAM4K and RAM16K add further levels until you reach the full 16K-word data memory. The key point is each level increases capacity by a factor of eight by stacking an additional 3-bit selection tier. This keeps the wiring regular and the design modular. A practical consequence is that debugging is easier: localize failures to one module level and test that layer's DMuxes and Muxes. One misconception is assuming address bits are distributed evenly across physical wires; instead think in logical partitions where each level consumes a fixed number of lower bits for local addressing. When implementing RAM16K, ensure your top-level address width supports 14 bits for 16K words (the Hack data memory uses a 15-bit address space overall for consistency with the ROM), and verify every submodule passes its tests before composing them. Takeaway: predictable expansion by fixed-size tiles is the heart of the R A M hierarchy.

keyIdea.title: Scaling principle
keyIdea.text: Each RAM level multiplies capacity by composing eight copies of the previous level and consuming another 3 address bits for selection.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › RAM Scaling

From RAM512 to RAM16K

Each new level composes eight copies of the previous RAM chip and consumes an extra 3 address bits to expand capacity eightfold.

RAM512
Built from eight RAM64 chips. Uses 9-bit addresses: 3 lower, 6 upper splitting across levels.
RAM4K
Built from eight RAM512 chips. Address width grows accordingly to select the correct subblock and inner register.
RAM16K
Final data memory for Hack: 16K words. Each higher-level DMux/Mux layer routes signals across blocks predictably.
Debugging strategy
Test each module individually. If a top-level read is wrong, isolate by checking outputs at every intermediate Mux level to find the failing submodule.
Misconception
Don't assume the address is a single opaque value; treat it as partitions consumed at each recursion layer for clear wiring and testing.

screens.title: Program Counter (PC) Basics
screens.narratorSegment: The Program Counter is a 16-bit register that holds the address of the next instruction. It has three control inputs: inc, load, and reset. On each clock cycle the PC produces a next value chosen by a chain of Mux16 operations: incrementing the current PC produces the next sequential address; loading allows external control to set the PC to a new address, typically for jumps; reset forces the PC to zero so execution can start or recover. The design gives priority to reset over load and load over inc: reset > load > inc. That ordering ensures the machine can always be brought to a known state, then perform deliberate control transfers, and otherwise continue sequentially. A concrete example: on a jump instruction the C P U asserts load with the jump target while inc remains active; because load outranks inc, the PC will load the jump target rather than incrementing. A common error is swapping priorities so that an increment could override a load, which would make jumps unreliable. Takeaway: the PC is a small register with a selection chain that enforces safe, predictable control flow.

keyIdea.title: PC priority
keyIdea.text: PC selects next value by priority: reset overrides load, and load overrides increment; this preserves initialization and reliable jumps.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Program Counter
Definition

PC: inc, load, reset

The PC is a register with logic to choose its next input: increment, explicit load, or reset to zero.

inc
When asserted, the PC increments by one on the next clock cycle.
load
When asserted, the PC loads the supplied input value on the next clock cycle.
reset
When asserted, the PC resets to zero regardless of other controls.
Example
Jump case: load=1 and inc=1. Because load outranks inc, the PC will load the target address instead of incrementing. Reset case: if reset=1, PC becomes 0 regardless of load or inc.
Key takeaway
Priority ordering is essential. Treat reset as emergency override, load as deliberate control, and inc as default progression.
Common mistake
If priorities are implemented incorrectly, jumps or resets may be ignored under concurrent signals.

screens.title: PC Selection Chain — Mux16 Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: The PC's next value is selected by a small chain of 16-bit multiplexers. Start with three candidates: hold (the register's current value), increment (hold plus one), and the external input. The selection chain proceeds in steps: first compute increment by feeding the current PC into an incrementer; then select between hold and increment using a Mux16 controlled by inc; next select between that result and the external input using a Mux16 controlled by load; finally select between the resulting value and zero using a Mux16 controlled by reset. This ordering implements reset > load > inc because reset is applied last and therefore overrides earlier choices. A concrete pseudo-structure you will implement follows this pattern: next = Mux16(hold, incResult, sel=inc); next = Mux16(next, in, sel=load); next = Mux16(next, 0, sel=reset); Register(in=next, load=true). When testing, simulate combinations where multiple control signals are high to confirm the priority behavior. A common pitfall is wiring the Muxes in the wrong order: placing reset early may let later signals override the reset. Takeaway: the chain order encodes priority; read it as 'start with default, then offer overrides in descending priority.'

keyIdea.title: Mux chain rule
keyIdea.text: Order the Mux16 operations so that higher-priority signals are applied last, ensuring they override lower-priority choices.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › PC Mux Chain
Code-like structure

PC selection chain

Implement the Mux16 chain so reset overrides load and load overrides inc.

// pseudo-structure for PC next value
// hold is current PC output
incResult = Add16(hold, 1)
next = Mux16(a=hold, b=incResult, sel=inc)
next = Mux16(a=next, b=in, sel=load)
next = Mux16(a=next, b=0, sel=reset)
// Register receives next on clock
Register(in=next, load=true)
Test scenario
Set inc=1, load=1, reset=0. Expect the PC to load the external input, not increment. Then set reset=1 and confirm PC becomes 0.
Concepts to watch
  • Compute inc result from current PC via Add16 or Inc16.
  • Chain Mux16 operations so higher-priority control is applied last.
  • Register feedback provides the hold input for the next cycle.

screens.title: Memory Map: RAM16K vs ROM32K
screens.narratorSegment: The Hack computer separates data memory and instruction memory into two address spaces. Data memory is provided by the RAM16K chip you build; it stores variables, arrays, and temporary values used by programs. Instruction memory is ROM32K, supplied by the simulator, which stores the program's instructions. Both memories are addressed by 15-bit addresses in the full system, but they are used differently: the C P U uses the PC to address instruction memory and uses a C P U-controlled address line to access data memory. A concrete implication is that writes go only to data memory while instruction memory remains read-only in normal operation. Another important point: the RAM16K you build must behave correctly when an address has never been written—tests expect uninitialized locations to return zero. A common misconception is thinking the C P U treats both memories interchangeably; in the Hack architecture they are distinct: ROM holds code, R A M holds mutable data. When integrating your memory components into the full computer, ensure the bus and control signals route reads and writes to the correct memory space. Takeaway: understand the separation of roles and verify that RAM16K meets data memory expectations while ROM32K is used for instruction fetches.

Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Memory Map

RAM16K (data) vs ROM32K (instructions)

Understand the separate roles each memory plays and how the CPU addresses them.

Data memory — RAM16K
Mutable storage built from RAM chips you implement. Tests expect uninitialized values to read as zero and writes to affect only the targeted address.
Instruction memory — ROM32K
Read-only program storage provided by the simulator; the PC addresses this space to fetch instructions.
Integration note
Ensure bus control routes writes only to RAM16K. Instruction fetches read from ROM32K via the PC; writes to ROM are not part of the Hack CPU operation.
Example check
Run a simple program that writes to RAM, then read the same address: RAM should reflect the written value while ROM remains unchanged.

screens.title: Testing RAM: Correctness Criteria
screens.narratorSegment: Testing R A M is crucial and often uncovers subtle wiring mistakes. There are three core correctness criteria the test scripts check. First, uninitialized locations should return zero. When your simulator resets or when a location has never been written, the R A M read should be 0. Second, writes to one address must not affect other addresses: this is write isolation. A test will write distinct values to different addresses and then read them back to ensure there is no cross-contamination. Third, sequential reads and writes across clock cycles must behave correctly: if you write to an address in one cycle and read it in the next, the updated value should be visible; conversely, reads in the same cycle as a write may see the prior value depending on the specified timing. In the Hack project tests the scripts are designed to exercise these cases. A common oversight is forgetting to zero unused registers or misrouting load signals so multiple registers receive writes. Diagnose failures by testing smaller modules: confirm each RAM8 works, then compose up. Takeaway: rigorous unit tests at each level and attention to DMux/Mux wiring produce reliable RAM16K that will integrate cleanly into the full computer.

screens.title: Assessment: PC Priority Question
screens.narratorSegment: One assessment asks why the PC priority order is reset > load > inc and what would happen if we changed it. The answer rests on safety and intent. Reset must override everything so the machine can be reliably initialized or forced to a known state in an emergency; if load outranked reset the reset signal could be ignored during a concurrent load, preventing recovery. Load must outrank increment because load implements explicit control transfers like jumps and subroutine returns; if inc outranked load then a jump instruction might be ignored and execution would continue sequentially, breaking program semantics. If priorities were wrongly implemented, programs relying on jumps or reset behavior would behave unpredictably. A concrete scenario illustrates this: suppose a jump instruction sets load=1 at the same time inc=1. With correct priority the PC accepts the jump target. With reversed priority the PC increments and the jump is lost. When you answer such a question, explain both the rationale and provide a specific failing example. This shows you understand not just the rule but its practical consequences. Takeaway: priority enforces predictable control flow and system recoverability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.6 › Assessment: PC Priority

Question walkthrough

Explain why reset > load > inc and show a concrete failure if the order changes.

Rationale
Reset ensures known starting state. Load implements deliberate control transfers. Inc is the default progression.
Failing scenario
If inc outranks load, a jump with load=1 and inc=1 would be ignored and the PC would increment, skipping the jump target.
Answer tip
When writing your answer, include the priority rule, the rationale for each rank, and a concrete example demonstrating the failure mode.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will complete the Hack computer's memory subsystem and build the components that let a C P U remember values and step through instructions. We will move from a single Bit and a 16-bit Register to a family of R A M chips built recursively, culminating in RAM16K as the Hack data memory. You will also assemble the Program Counter, which chooses between holding its value, loading a new address, incrementing, or resetting to zero. These pieces are essential because memory and the program counter control program flow and data storage in the von Neumann architecture. For example, when executing a jump instruction the C P U asserts the PC's load input so the next instruction comes from a new address; when starting the system the reset input ensures execution begins at address zero. As you build each R A M level, you'll see the same small building blocks repeated and combined using DMux and Mux chips to route addresses and data. By the end of Project 3 you will have tested read/write isolation, correct uninitialized behavior, and the PC selection priority. Think about why reset must override load and increment — that's the safety that lets a machine recover to a known state.

By the end of Project 3 you will have four verified competencies. First, you will complete the sequential chips that the Hack C P U needs to hold state: implement the Bit primitive and the 16-bit Register and understand how load gates control writing on the clock. Second, you will assemble the R A M family up to RAM16K by composing smaller R A M chips recursively; you will explain how lower and upper address bits are used to select the right subchip. Third, you will design and test the Program Counter with three controls — increment, load, and reset — and understand why the reset > load > inc priority is essential for predictable startup and jumps. Fourth, you will prepare for higher-level architecture work by ensuring your memory components pass tests for uninitialized reads, write isolation, and sequential read/write behavior. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic and a verified competency milestone you can use as a checkpoint in the simulator.

This screen turns objectives into concrete actions you will perform in the simulator. For the sequential chips, you will compile and run tests that check a Bit and a Register respond to clocked load signals. For recursive R A M construction, you will implement RAM8 and then reuse it to make RAM64 and larger chips, showing how lower address bits index inside a chip while upper bits select which subchip is active. For the PC, you will wire Mux16 and Add16 so that the Register receives the correct next value under reset, load, and increment conditions; you will also run the PC test to observe the reset behavior and jump loads. For testing memory, follow the provided test scripts: verify uninitialized locations return 0, writes only affect the addressed location, and reads after writes behave as expected across clock cycles. Each hands-on step maps to a verified competency milestone in the learning plan. Keep the test scripts green before moving on to computer architecture.

Begin with the Bit primitive: a single flip-flop that stores one binary value across clock cycles. In the Hack design the Bit is built from a D flip-flop with a Mux that selects between the existing value and the input gated by the load signal. That small pattern is the building block for registers. A 16-bit Register is simply sixteen Bit chips wired in parallel, all sharing the same load and clock signals so they write together. Concretely, when load is 1 the Mux forwards the D inputs into the flip-flops on the rising clock edge; when load is 0 each Bit feeds back its current output, so the register holds its previous value. A common misconception is thinking each bit can be written independently inside a register; in this design the entire 16-bit vector updates together under a single load. A practical example: to store the constant address 123 into a register, set the register's input bus to the 16-bit representation of 123 and assert load for one clock tick—after the tick the register holds 123. Key checks while implementing: confirm each Bit holds its state when load is 0, and that toggling load writes all 16 bits in sync. Takeaway: small, verified flip-flops compose predictably into wider registers.

RAM8 is the first composite R A M chip: it contains eight 16-bit registers and an address width of three bits. The three-bit address directly selects which of the eight registers drives the output and which register receives a write. This selection is implemented with DMuxes that split the load signal by address and with Muxes that combine each register's output into a single 16-bit bus. The pattern is straightforward: the lower-level registers are identical, and DMux logic ensures only the targeted register sees the load on a write cycle. A concrete example: if address 010 is presented and load is 1 during the clock, the DMux routes the load to register number two; that register latches the input value while the others hold. A common misconception is thinking Muxes copy values in hardware; rather they steer buses so only the selected register's output appears on the shared output bus. In practice, implement RAM8 by instantiating eight Register chips, use a 3-way DMux tree for write selection, and a 3-way Mux tree for read aggregation. Takeaway: RAM8 shows the basic pattern you will replicate recursively to build larger R A M chips.

The power of recursion becomes clear when you build RAM64 from RAM8 blocks. RAM64 contains eight RAM8 chips and uses a six-bit address. The address is partitioned: the lower three bits select a register within a RAM8 block, and the upper three bits select which of the eight RAM8 chips to enable. On a write, the RAM64 DMux tree uses the upper address bits to route the overall load to exactly one RAM8 chip; that chip's internal DMuxes then route the load to the targeted register inside it. On a read, a two-level Mux tree first selects the output from each RAM8 using the lower bits and then selects among these eight outputs using the upper bits. This approach generalizes: RAM512 uses nine-bit addressing (lower 3 bits intra-chip, upper 6 bits to choose which RAM64 block), and higher levels follow the same split. A concrete example: to write at address 0b001011 you route load to the RAM8 specified by upper bits 001 and inside that RAM8 use lower bits 011 to address the register. A useful mental model is a tree of identical modules: the same small unit repeats at every node. Misunderstanding often comes from confusing which bits are 'upper' vs 'lower'—draw the bit positions to avoid that error. Takeaway: recursion simplifies wiring by reusing tested components and predictable address partitioning.

Scaling beyond RAM64 follows the same architectural pattern: add more address bits and compose larger blocks from smaller ones. RAM512 uses nine address bits and is built from eight RAM64 modules; the lower three bits still select a register within a RAM8, the next three pick the RAM8 inside a RAM64, and the upper three choose which RAM64 block to enable. Continuing this pattern, RAM4K and RAM16K add further levels until you reach the full 16K-word data memory. The key point is each level increases capacity by a factor of eight by stacking an additional 3-bit selection tier. This keeps the wiring regular and the design modular. A practical consequence is that debugging is easier: localize failures to one module level and test that layer's DMuxes and Muxes. One misconception is assuming address bits are distributed evenly across physical wires; instead think in logical partitions where each level consumes a fixed number of lower bits for local addressing. When implementing RAM16K, ensure your top-level address width supports 14 bits for 16K words (the Hack data memory uses a 15-bit address space overall for consistency with the ROM), and verify every submodule passes its tests before composing them. Takeaway: predictable expansion by fixed-size tiles is the heart of the R A M hierarchy.

The Program Counter is a 16-bit register that holds the address of the next instruction. It has three control inputs: inc, load, and reset. On each clock cycle the PC produces a next value chosen by a chain of Mux16 operations: incrementing the current PC produces the next sequential address; loading allows external control to set the PC to a new address, typically for jumps; reset forces the PC to zero so execution can start or recover. The design gives priority to reset over load and load over inc: reset > load > inc. That ordering ensures the machine can always be brought to a known state, then perform deliberate control transfers, and otherwise continue sequentially. A concrete example: on a jump instruction the C P U asserts load with the jump target while inc remains active; because load outranks inc, the PC will load the jump target rather than incrementing. A common error is swapping priorities so that an increment could override a load, which would make jumps unreliable. Takeaway: the PC is a small register with a selection chain that enforces safe, predictable control flow.

The PC's next value is selected by a small chain of 16-bit multiplexers. Start with three candidates: hold (the register's current value), increment (hold plus one), and the external input. The selection chain proceeds in steps: first compute increment by feeding the current PC into an incrementer; then select between hold and increment using a Mux16 controlled by inc; next select between that result and the external input using a Mux16 controlled by load; finally select between the resulting value and zero using a Mux16 controlled by reset. This ordering implements reset > load > inc because reset is applied last and therefore overrides earlier choices. A concrete pseudo-structure you will implement follows this pattern: next = Mux16(hold, incResult, sel=inc); next = Mux16(next, in, sel=load); next = Mux16(next, 0, sel=reset); Register(in=next, load=true). When testing, simulate combinations where multiple control signals are high to confirm the priority behavior. A common pitfall is wiring the Muxes in the wrong order: placing reset early may let later signals override the reset. Takeaway: the chain order encodes priority; read it as 'start with default, then offer overrides in descending priority.'

The Hack computer separates data memory and instruction memory into two address spaces. Data memory is provided by the RAM16K chip you build; it stores variables, arrays, and temporary values used by programs. Instruction memory is ROM32K, supplied by the simulator, which stores the program's instructions.
